A 55-year-old man presents to the emergency department with nausea and vomiting for the past week. He decided to come in when his symptoms worsened. He feels that his symptoms are exacerbated with large fatty meals and when he drinks alcohol. His wife recently returned from a cruise with symptoms of vomiting and diarrhea. The patient has a medical history of poorly managed diabetes, constipation, anxiety, dyslipidemia, and hypertension. His temperature is 99.5°F (37.5°C), blood pressure is 197/128 mmHg, pulse is 100/min, respirations are 17/min, and oxygen saturation is 95% on room air. Physical exam reveals a systolic murmur heard loudest along the left upper sternal border. Abdominal exam reveals an obese, tympanitic and distended abdomen with a 3 cm scar in the right lower quadrant. Vascular exam reveals weak pulses in the lower extremities. Which of the following is the most likely underlying etiology of this patient's symptoms?

Options:
A. Adhesions
B. Enteric nervous system damage
C. Impacted stool
D. Norovirus
E. Twisting of the bowel

Patient with IBD, particularly Crohn’s disease, are at increased risk of SIBO. In a systematic review and meta-analysis, the proportion of SIBO in patients with IBD was 22.3% (95% CI 19.92–24.68). The odds ratio (OR) for SIBO in patients with IBD was 9.51 (95% CI 3.39–26.68) compared to controls without IBD. The OR was significantly elevated in both CD (OR 10.86; 95% CI 2.76–42.69) and UC (OR 7.96; 95% CI 1.66–38.35). In subgroup analysis, patients with fibrostenosing CD (OR 7.47; 95% CI 2.51–22.20) and prior bowel surgery (OR 2.38; 95% CI 1.65–3.44), had increased odds of SIBO. Diagnosing SUI based on classic symptoms can be easily confirmed during pelvic examination, by asking the patient to cough or Valsalva with a full bladder. If the provider observes urine leaking from the urethra during an office cough/Valsalva stress test, the diagnosis of SUI is confirmed. Urodynamic testing can also be performed to confirm a suspected diagnosis of SUI, however, based on the Value of Urodynamic Evaluation study, in women with uncomplicated SUI without significant prolapse or urinary urgency, if SUI is demonstrated on examination, additional urodynamic testing is not necessary before treatment. UUI is diagnosed by history and ensuring no acute cystitis, a normal post-void residual and normal screening urinalysis. Urodynamic testing may be considered if there are new-onset urinary symptoms and concern for pelvic nerve injury, such as in the setting of a prolonged second stage of labor or operative vaginal delivery. In women who have suspected bladder overdistension injury, urodynamics could help with diagnosis and determining prognosis, however, they are not mandatory.

Presentation: An 83-year-old man with a history of hypertension and asthma, and no prior abdominal surgeries, presented to the Department of General Surgery with an 8 × 8 cm necrotic area at the scrotal base. Nineteen years earlier, the patient had received radiation therapy twice over four years, totaling 82 Gy, for a condition in the same region. The patient was evaluated by colorectal surgeons, plastic surgeons, and urologists. The lesion was located at the scrotal base and featured a necrotic ulcer in the perianal area. Initial assessments considered the condition as a potential side effect of previous radiation therapy. Multiple biopsies were performed, and histopathological examination revealed specific findings without signs of invasiveness. Further clinical workup, including a normal colonoscopy and MRI of the lower abdomen, ruled out involvement of the urethra or corpora cavernosum.. Confirmed diagnosis: Primary perianal Paget’s disease. Differential diagnosis includes: Primary perianal Paget’s disease.

Presentation: A 42-year-old male with a history of cervical spine injury resulting in paraplegia since adolescence and end-stage renal disease on hemodialysis, as well as a small bowel obstruction treated with lysis of adhesions six months prior, presented with chronic abdominal pain and progressive abdominal distension over three months. His vital signs were stable and he was afebrile. Physical examination revealed a markedly tense abdomen with generalized tenderness and dullness on percussion. No signs of chronic liver disease were noted. Given his history of small bowel obstruction and the severity of his pain, a contrast-enhanced computed tomography (CT) scan of the abdomen and pelvis was performed. The CT scan showed no obstruction or perforation but revealed a large amount of loculated ascites, multiple adhesions with small bowel loops tethered to these adhesions, and hepatomegaly without evidence of cirrhosis or biliary tract obstruction. Laboratory results were as follows: calcium 8.7 mg/dL, alkaline phosphatase 650 IU/L, total bilirubin 0.9 mg/dL, direct bilirubin 0.6 mg/dL, albumin 2 g/dL, globulin 5.3 g/dL, aspartate transaminase 20 IU/L, alanine transaminase 33 IU/L, and internationa. Confirmed diagnosis: Hepatic transthyretin amyloidosis. Differential diagnosis includes: Hepatic transthyretin amyloidosis.

Presentation: A 48-year-old male was admitted to Beijing YouAn Hospital with liver cirrhosis. Four months prior, an abdominal ultrasound indicated cirrhosis and splenomegaly, despite the patient experiencing no discomfort. At another hospital, he was diagnosed with diabetes and started on insulin therapy. The patient reported minimal alcohol consumption and no family history of liver diseases. Physical examination revealed skin pigmentation but no other abnormalities. Liver function tests showed elevated levels of alanine aminotransferase (ALT) and aspartate aminotransferase (AST). Serum markers for viral hepatitis and autoimmune liver diseases were negative. Plasma iron indices were abnormal: iron at 47 μmol/L, transferrin saturation at 97.9%, and ferritin levels exceeding 2000 ng/ml. HbA1c was significantly elevated, while testosterone levels were normal at 18.26 nmol/L. Pre-contrast computed tomography (CT) showed hepatomegaly with increased attenuation in the liver and spleen, splenomegaly, and formation of collateral circulation. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) demonstrated a typical decrease in T2-weighted signal intensity over the liver.. Confirmed diagnosis: Type 3 Hemochromatosis. Differential diagnosis includes: Type 3 Hemochromatosis.

Presentation: A 55-year-old Caucasian male with a history of multiple myeloma currently undergoing chemotherapy with Velcade, Cytoxan, and dexamethasone, chronic kidney disease, hypertension, atrial flutter post-ablation, and melanoma of the left thigh post-surgical resection with negative lymph nodes and in remission, presented to the hospital with multiple episodes of nausea and vomiting, diffuse abdominal pain, subjective fevers, and chills over the past 2 days. His last bowel movement was 2 days ago. On presentation, his vitals were stable. Laboratory tests, including a complete blood count and comprehensive metabolic panel, were normal. A CT scan of the abdomen and pelvis without contrast showed a partial small bowel obstruction. A small bowel follow-through indicated non-specific thickening of the proximal small bowel loops. This was his third hospitalization with the same presentation of small bowel obstruction, with previous admissions one month ago and 2 weeks ago. During the initial hospitalization, an exploratory laparotomy showed no findings to suggest mechanical small bowel obstruction. An esophagogastroduodenoscopy (EGD) with push enteroscopy identified enteritis and a Mallory-Weis. Confirmed diagnosis: Gastrointestinal Amyloidosis. Differential diagnosis includes: Gastrointestinal Amyloidosis.

Presentation: A three-day-old newborn male presented to the emergency department with abdominal distension and bilious vomiting starting on the second day after birth. Direct abdominal radiography and abdominal ultrasound did not reveal any abnormalities. Routine laboratory tests and thyroid hormone levels were within normal limits. A contrast enema radiography was conducted to investigate neonatal congenital bowel issues, but no abnormalities were detected. The patient resumed normal oral feeding for two days, after which vomiting recurred. Nasogastric intubation produced drainage containing fecalith, and there was an increase in abdominal distension, leading to the decision for an emergency operation.. Confirmed diagnosis: Ileum Duplication Cyst. Differential diagnosis includes: Ileum Duplication Cyst.

If the provider observes urine leaking from the urethra during an office cough/Valsalva stress test, the diagnosis of SUI is confirmed. Presentation: A 55-year-old Caucasian male with a history of multiple myeloma currently undergoing chemotherapy with Velcade, Cytoxan, and dexamethasone, chronic kidney disease, hypertension, atrial flutter post-ablation, and melanoma of the left thigh post-surgical resection with negative lymph nodes and in remission, presented to the hospital with multiple episodes of nausea and vomiting, diffuse abdominal pain, subjective fevers, and chills over the past 2 days. Presentation: A three-day-old newborn male presented to the emergency department with abdominal distension and bilious vomiting starting on the second day after birth.
